title: Alfama on foot: from Lisbon Cathedral up to the castle and the viewpoints, what is free, and tram 28
subtitle: A climb of a kilometre and a half through the oldest quarter of Lisbon, with one ticket most people buy and a tram most people can skip.
excerpt: The route from the cathedral up to the Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol viewpoints and the São Jorge Castle, what is free and what needs a ticket in Alfama, how to use tram 28 without the queue, and what the audio walks our partner sells include.
longtail_phrases: how to walk from Lisbon Cathedral to the castle
is São Jorge Castle worth the ticket
is tram 28 worth it
what is free in Alfama
is Lisbon Cathedral free to enter
meta_title: Alfama on foot: cathedral, castle, viewpoints, tram 28
meta_description: A walking route through Alfama from Lisbon Cathedral to the castle: what is free, what needs a ticket, and how to ride tram 28 without the queue.

featured_image.alt: The red roofs and white houses of Alfama below the towers of São Vicente de Fora, seen from the Portas do Sol viewpoint in Lisbon

content_html:
[place attraction="lisbon-cathedral" city="lisbon"]

In the summer of 1147 a fleet of crusaders from England, Flanders and the Rhineland, bound for the Holy Land, put in at Porto. Afonso Henriques, the first king of Portugal, persuaded them to stop on the way and help him take Lisbon from its Moorish rulers. When the city fell that October, an English priest from the fleet, Gilbert of Hastings, was made its bishop, and a cathedral was begun, by tradition on the site of the main mosque.

The slope between that cathedral and the castle above it is Alfama. The name is Arabic, from the hot springs that rose at the foot of the hill. Its lanes are too steep and narrow for cars, and the earthquake of 1755 did less harm here than in the lower town, so the medieval street plan survives. You can walk it in half a day, and most of it is free. The questions are which doors to pay at, and whether the famous tram is worth the wait.

The route in short

From the cathedral to the castle gate is about a kilometre and a half, all of it uphill, on cobbles.

  • Start at the church of St Anthony and the cathedral, which face each other across a small square.
  • Follow the tram tracks uphill for ten minutes to the Santa Luzia viewpoint, and one minute more to Portas do Sol.
  • Turn inland and climb the last streets to the São Jorge Castle.
  • Come down by the stairs and lanes of lower Alfama to the river, where the Fado Museum stands.

Allow three to four hours with the castle, two without.

The cathedral and St Anthony

The small church of St Anthony stands where, by tradition, Fernando de Bulhões was born around 1195. He became a Franciscan and is known to the world as Anthony of Padua, after the city where he died in 1231. The present church was built after the earthquake. Entry is free.

The cathedral, the Sé, looks like a fortress: two battlemented towers and a rose window between them. Inside are a Gothic cloister, where excavations have uncovered Roman and Moorish remains, and a treasury upstairs. For many years the nave was free and only the cloister and treasury were charged. More recently the cathedral has sold one visitor ticket for the building, while people coming to pray or to a service enter free. Check at the door.

The west front of the cathedral, begun after 1147. Photo: Threeohsix, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The two viewpoints

Santa Luzia is a terrace under a pergola beside a small church. Two tile panels on the church wall are worth a look: one shows the great riverside square as it was before 1755, the other the assault on the castle in 1147. Portas do Sol, a few steps on, is wider and has a statue of St Vincent, the patron of the city, holding a ship with two ravens. From both you look over the roofs to the dome of the National Pantheon and the river. Both are free at any hour. By mid-morning the tour groups arrive, so come early or towards evening.

Alfama and the Tagus from the Santa Luzia viewpoint. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The castle: the ticket most people buy

The São Jorge Castle was the Moorish citadel and then, from the thirteenth century, a royal residence, until King Manuel I moved the court down to a new palace by the river early in the sixteenth century. Much of what you walk on today comes from a heavy restoration around 1940, which cleared the later buildings and rebuilt the battlements.

The ticket covers the terrace with the widest view in Lisbon, the walk around the ramparts and towers, a small museum, an archaeological site with the remains of Moorish houses, and a camera obscura in one of the towers. Allow an hour and a half. The line at the ticket office is longest from late morning, so go at opening time or late in the afternoon.

Without a ticket you can walk the few streets inside the outer gate, but you will not reach the walls or the view.

The walls of the castle. Much of what stands was rebuilt around 1940. Photo: deror_avi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Tram 28

Line 28 runs from Martim Moniz to Campo de Ourique, through Graça, Alfama, the lower town, Chiado and Estrela. Its small wooden trams date from the 1930s: nothing larger can take the curves. It is an ordinary city line: the fare paid on board is higher than the one charged to a rechargeable transport card, and a day pass covers it.

In season the wait at Martim Moniz can pass an hour, the cars are packed, and the line is known for pickpockets. Three ways round that:

  • Ride early in the morning or in the evening.
  • Board at the other end, Campo de Ourique, where there is seldom a queue.
  • Do not ride it at all on this walk. The stretch from the cathedral to Portas do Sol takes ten minutes on foot, and you see the trams squeeze past you.

If the climb is the problem, a small city bus has run from Praça da Figueira up to the castle gate.

The track of tram 28 on its way through Alfama. Photo: Sonse, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What is free and what needs a ticket

  • Free: the lanes, both viewpoints and the two higher ones in Graça, the church of St Anthony, the church of São Vicente de Fora, and the flea market behind it, the Feira da Ladra, on Tuesdays and Saturdays.
  • Ticket: the castle; the cathedral as a visitor; the monastery of São Vicente de Fora, with its tiled cloisters and roof terrace; the National Pantheon, a church begun in 1682 and finished only in 1966; the Fado Museum; the museum of the Roman theatre.

What our partner sells here: audio walks, not tickets

For Alfama our partner sells only self-guided audio walks: recorded commentary and a map with your position, in the partner's app on your own phone. None of them includes entry to the castle, the cathedral or anything else, and you bring your own earphones. They differ in direction and length:

  • Alfama's Historic Heart, about two hours, climbs from the riverside past St Anthony and the cathedral, through the lower lanes to Portas do Sol, and ends in Graça. It is the closest to the route above.
  • Hills, Stones, and Squares starts at the castle and goes downhill past the cathedral to the river and on into Chiado. It fits well after a castle visit.
  • Chiado and Castle Heights and Chiado and Alfama both begin across the valley in Chiado and are longer. Hillside Lisbon is an overview of four districts.

These are the audio walks our partner sells for Alfama and the castle hill, with today's prices:

[partner city="lisbon" match="alfama,historic,castle,hills" limit="5"]

From here

At the foot of the hill, the Fado Museum tells the story of the city's music. Further east along the river, the National Tile Museum fills an old convent. Hours for the two main sights are on our pages for Lisbon Cathedral and the São Jorge Castle. See what else there is in Lisbon, or open the trip planner for Portugal.

Cover photo: Palickap, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk from Lisbon Cathedral to the castle?
faqs.a: About half an hour of steady uphill walking, a kilometre and a half on cobbles. With stops at the two viewpoints and a castle visit, allow three to four hours.

faqs.q: Is São Jorge Castle worth the ticket?
faqs.a: For the view, yes: its terrace and ramparts look over the whole centre of Lisbon and the river. Do not expect furnished rooms. The walls were largely rebuilt around 1940.

faqs.q: Is tram 28 worth it?
faqs.a: As a ride, early in the morning or in the evening. In the middle of the day the wait at Martim Moniz can pass an hour and the trams are packed. Boarding at Campo de Ourique avoids most of the queue.

faqs.q: What is free in Alfama?
faqs.a: The lanes, the Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol viewpoints, the church of St Anthony and the Feira da Ladra flea market on Tuesdays and Saturdays. The castle, the monastery of São Vicente de Fora and the National Pantheon charge for entry.

faqs.q: Is Lisbon Cathedral free to enter?
faqs.a: It is free for prayer and services. Visitors have been charged a ticket in recent years, which also covers the treasury, so check at the door.

title: Estádio da Luz and the Benfica Museum: stadium tour, museum or both, and what the bundles add
subtitle: Two visits behind two doors, six tickets that combine them with scarves, snacks and wine, and a metro line that goes straight there.
excerpt: What the Estádio da Luz tour shows, what is in the Benfica Museum, which of the two to choose, what the scarf, snack, wine and meal bundles add, how to get there by metro, and why to avoid a match day.
focus_keyword: Estádio da Luz tour or Benfica Museum
secondary_keywords: Estádio da Luz scarf offer ticket
longtail_phrases: is the Benfica stadium tour worth it
how long does the Estádio da Luz tour take
how to get to Estádio da Luz by metro
can you visit Estádio da Luz on a match day
is the Benfica Museum included in the stadium tour
meta_title: Estádio da Luz tour or Benfica Museum: which ticket
meta_description: The Benfica stadium tour, the museum or both: what each shows, what the scarf, snack and meal bundles add, the metro stop, and match day limits.

featured_image.alt: The Estádio da Luz in Lisbon from outside: a low oval stadium under a white roof hung from red steel arches

content_html:
[place attraction="igreja-de-nossa-senhora-da-luz-carnide" city="lisbon"]

Luz means light, but the home of Benfica is not named after its floodlights. It takes its name from the part of Lisbon it stands in, and that takes its name from a sixteenth-century church a short walk away, dedicated to Our Lady of Light. The club itself was founded in 1904 on the other side of the city, in Belém, and moved from ground to ground for half a century before it opened a stadium of its own here on 1 December 1954.

That first Estádio da Luz grew until it held about 120,000 people, which made it one of the largest stadiums in Europe. It was pulled down in stages, and the present one was built on the same site and opened on 25 October 2003, in time for the European Championship of 2004. Portugal lost the final here to Greece. The Champions League final was played here in 2014 and again in 2020, the second time to empty stands. On any day without a match you can walk in, and the first thing to settle is which of two visits you want.

Two visits, two doors

  • The stadium tour: the building itself, from the stands down to the grass.
  • The Benfica Museum, named after Cosme Damião, one of the founders. It opened in 2013 in a building of its own beside the stadium.

Each has its own ticket, and there is a combined one. Outside, free to see, are the bronze statue of Eusébio, where supporters leave scarves, and the club shop.

The statue of Eusébio outside the stadium, free to see. Photo: Erik Cleves Kristensen, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The stadium tour

The tour is not led by a guide from start to finish. As our partner's listing describes it, you swap your voucher at Gate 17 and follow a marked route at your own pace, with staff posted at some of the stops to explain and answer questions. The stops listed are:

  • scale models of the stadium and of the club's training campus;
  • a stand and one of the lounges;
  • the visitors' dressing room (the listing does not name the home one);
  • the press conference room;
  • a hall of fame, with a virtual reality film;
  • the players' tunnel and the edge of the pitch;
  • the eagles.

The eagles are real. Before home matches one of them is released to fly around the bowl and land on the club's crest, and the birds are kept at the stadium. The route ends in the shop. Allow about an hour.

What you remember is the bowl: some 65,000 red seats in tiers under a roof that hangs from four steel arches.

The view from pitch level, the last stop of the stadium tour. Photo: Threeohsix, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The museum

The museum has 29 themed areas on three floors. It covers every sport the club plays, not only football, and it sets the club's story beside that of Lisbon and Portugal in the same years. The best rooms are about the early 1960s, when Benfica, coached by the Hungarian Béla Guttmann, won the European Cup in 1961 and 1962, the second time against Real Madrid.

The player of those years was Eusébio. Born in Mozambique in 1942, he joined the club at eighteen, won the Ballon d'Or in 1965 and was top scorer at the World Cup of 1966 with nine goals. He died in 2014 and now lies in the National Pantheon. The museum also has screens, a simulator and a penalty shoot-out game, which is where children spend their time. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.

The European Cups of 1961 and 1962 in the museum. Photo: Threeohsix, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Stadium, museum or both

  • You have one hour, or only one of you follows football: the stadium tour. The building impresses people who do not care about the club.
  • You are a supporter, of Benfica or of the game: both. Together they take about two and a half hours.
  • You are with small children: the tour for the pitch and the eagles. Add the museum only if they like the games.
  • It is raining: the museum is fully indoors. Most of the tour is under cover, but the pitchside is open.

What the bundles add

Our partner lists six tickets. Under the names there are only three visits: the stadium, the museum, and the two together. The rest is extras.

  • Scarf offer. A club scarf handed over with your ticket. It comes with the stadium ticket, the museum ticket and most of the combined ones.
  • Wine tasting. The combined ticket, a scarf, and a tasting at a bar in the stadium's shopping area.
  • Snack. The combined ticket, a scarf and a snack. The listing does not say what the snack is.
  • Meal. The combined ticket with a voucher towards a meal at the stadium's restaurant. It is a voucher of a fixed value, not a set menu, the restaurant must be reserved, and no scarf is listed.

The visit is the same in all of them. Choose the plain combined ticket unless you would have bought the extra anyway. Transport is not included in any.

These are the stadium and museum tickets our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="lisbon" match="scarf,estadio,benfica" limit="6"]

Getting there by metro

The blue line of the Lisbon metro runs from the centre (Baixa-Chiado, Restauradores, Marquês de Pombal) straight to the stadium in about a quarter of an hour, with no change. Two stations serve it: Alto dos Moinhos, and one stop further Colégio Militar/Luz, which opens into the Colombo shopping centre. From either it is a walk of five to ten minutes. Gate 17, where vouchers are exchanged, is signed on the outside of the stadium.

Match days

A stadium in use is not a museum. On the day of a home match the tour has been cut short or closed, and areas such as the dressing rooms and the pitchside can be out of bounds from the day before a European game. The listing does not spell out the rule. So look at the club's fixture list before you choose a date, and keep away from match days and the days around big games.

If what you want is to see a match, that is a different purchase: match tickets are sold by the club and are not part of any ticket described here.

From here

Colombo, across the road, is one of the largest shopping centres in the country and the easy place to eat. Three stops back towards the centre on the same line is Jardim Zoológico, for the Lisbon Zoo. In the other direction, ten minutes on foot, is the old village of Carnide and the church of Our Lady of Light that gave the stadium its name. See what else there is in Lisbon, or open the trip planner for Portugal.

Cover photo: Alvesgaspar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Is the Benfica stadium tour worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like football or large buildings. In about an hour you see the stands, a dressing room, the press room, the tunnel and the edge of the pitch of a stadium that has hosted a European Championship final and two Champions League finals.

faqs.q: How long does the Estádio da Luz tour take?
faqs.a: About an hour for the stadium tour and an hour to an hour and a half for the museum. Allow two and a half hours for both.

faqs.q: How do you get to Estádio da Luz by metro?
faqs.a: Take the blue line from the centre to Alto dos Moinhos or Colégio Militar/Luz. The ride takes about a quarter of an hour and the stadium is five to ten minutes on foot from either station.

faqs.q: Can you visit Estádio da Luz on a match day?
faqs.a: The tour has been shortened or closed on home match days, and parts of it can be closed around big games. Check the fixture list and choose another day.

faqs.q: Is the Benfica Museum included in the stadium tour?
faqs.a: No. The museum and the stadium tour have separate tickets. A combined ticket covers both, and it is the one most of the bundles are built on.

title: PortAventura or Ferrari Land from Barcelona: which park, the combined ticket, and the train
subtitle: Two gates side by side on the coast south of Barcelona, three kinds of ticket, and a railway station of their own.
excerpt: What PortAventura Park and Ferrari Land each offer, which one to choose with small children or with teenagers, what the single and combined tickets include and leave out, and how the train from Barcelona works.
secondary_keywords: PortAventura and Ferrari Land combined ticket
longtail_phrases: is Ferrari Land worth it on its own
can you do PortAventura and Ferrari Land in one day
how to get to PortAventura from Barcelona by train
does the PortAventura ticket include the water park
how far is the Port Aventura train station from the park
meta_title: PortAventura or Ferrari Land from Barcelona: which ticket
meta_description: PortAventura Park, Ferrari Land or both in one day: what each ticket includes, which park suits which age, and how the train from Barcelona works.

featured_image.alt: The red loops of the Dragon Khan roller coaster and the tall white track of Shambhala against a blue sky at PortAventura Park

content_html:
[place attraction="portaventura-park" city="salou"]

On 1 May 1995 a theme park opened on farmland behind the beach town of Salou, an hour and a half down the coast from Barcelona. Spain had fairgrounds and small amusement parks, but nothing of this size. Its showpiece was Dragon Khan, a red and white roller coaster that turned its riders upside down eight times, which no coaster in the world had done before.

Thirty years on, PortAventura is the most visited theme park in Spain and has become a resort: three parks, a row of hotels and a railway station that carries its name. For a visitor staying in Barcelona, about a hundred kilometres away, that leaves two decisions. Which gate do you buy a ticket for, and is the train a sensible way to get there?

Three parks, three tickets

  • PortAventura Park is the original and by far the largest. It is laid out as a journey through six areas: Mediterrània at the gate, then Polynesia, China, México and the Far West, with SésamoAventura for small children. It needs a full day.
  • Ferrari Land opened next door in 2017, with a gate of its own. It is much smaller: a handful of rides around a square of copied Italian buildings. Two to three hours cover it.
  • Caribe Aquatic Park is a water park, open in the summer months only, with a separate ticket. Our partner does not sell it.

The lake of Mediterrània, the area just inside the gate. Photo: Alberto-g-rovi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What is in each

PortAventura Park

The big coasters are at the far end, in China: Dragon Khan and, wrapped around it, Shambhala, which opened in 2012 with a first drop from 76 metres. Near the gate, Furius Baco launches its trains instead of lifting them. The Far West has a wooden racing coaster and the water rides that everyone wants on a hot afternoon. Between the rides there are shows through the day, and they are included in the ticket.

The Far West area, dressed for the Halloween season. Photo: Alberto-g-rovi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

Ferrari Land

One ride is the reason to come: Red Force, a single tower 112 metres high, up which a train is fired at 180 kilometres an hour in five seconds. It was the tallest and fastest coaster in Europe when it opened. Around it are two drop towers, a family racing ride, simulators and a small area for children. If Red Force is closed, for wind or for maintenance, there is not much left for an adult.

Ferrari Land, with the tower of Red Force on the right. Photo: Ahs 34000, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which park

  • First visit, one day: PortAventura Park alone. It already holds more than a day can.
  • Teenagers and coaster fans: the combined ticket. Ferrari Land has often kept shorter hours than the main park, so check the hours for your date and fit Red Force into them.
  • Small children: PortAventura Park, for SésamoAventura and the shows. Ferrari Land has little for them.
  • Ferrari Land alone: only if you already know the main park, or have just an afternoon.

Height matters more than age. The partner's listing notes that some coasters ask for a minimum height of between 1.20 and 1.40 metres, and a maximum of 1.95. Measure your children before you promise them a ride.

What the tickets include, and what they leave out

All three tickets our partner sells work the same way: one day in the park or parks named, on the date you choose, with the rides and the regular shows. A change of date may be possible within the same season. Children under four go in free.

What none of them includes:

  • The fast pass. The park sells its own express passes for the ride queues. On a busy day they decide how many of the big coasters you get onto. They are bought separately.
  • The water park, lockers, parking, food and drink.
  • Some special-event shows, which can carry a charge of their own.

"Direct entrance" in the names means you skip the ticket office and go to the turnstiles with the voucher on your phone. It does not shorten any queue inside.

These are the tickets our partner sells for the two parks, and for two quieter places nearby, with today's prices:

[partner city="tarragona" match="portaventura,ferrari" limit="5"]

The train from Barcelona

Regional trains of the Rodalies network leave from Barcelona Sants, and also stop at Passeig de Gràcia, run down the coast through Tarragona and end at a station called Port Aventura. The journey takes about an hour and a half.

  • Trains are not frequent. Choose your outward and return trains before you set out, and note the last one back: on long summer evenings it can leave before the park closes.
  • From the platform to the gates is about a kilometre on a signposted path.
  • The high-speed station called Camp de Tarragona is far inland and has no easy link to the park. Do not book to it.
  • This line has been interrupted by engineering works several times in recent years, with buses replacing trains on part of the way. Check the day before.

By car the drive takes a little over an hour on the motorway, and parking is charged. Coaches also run from Barcelona to Salou.

The Port Aventura station, about a kilometre from the gates. Photo: 9pm, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Planning the day

Be at the gate for opening. Most people stop at the first big ride they meet, so walk straight to the back of the park and ride Shambhala and Dragon Khan first. Keep the water rides for the heat of the afternoon and the shows for the middle of the day, when the queues are longest. The park is not open all year: it has closed for the weeks after early January, and in spring and autumn it shuts on some weekdays. Look at the calendar before you book anything else. Hours are on our pages for PortAventura Park and Ferrari Land.

From here

The beaches of Salou are two kilometres from the gates. Tarragona, ten kilometres north, was the Roman capital of this coast: its amphitheatre stands above the sea, and the cathedral at the top of the old town has a fine cloister. Our partner sells its entry with an audio guide, the bell tower excepted. Near Cambrils, Parc Samà is a garden laid out in 1881 for a family that had made its fortune in Cuba, with a lake, a grotto and peacocks. Open the trip planner for Spain to fit them together.

Cover photo: Artistosteles, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is Ferrari Land worth it on its own?
faqs.a: Only for coaster fans who want Red Force, or if you already know the main park. It is small, two to three hours cover it, and it has little for young children.

faqs.q: Can you do PortAventura Park and Ferrari Land in one day?
faqs.a: Yes, with the combined ticket, if you arrive at opening and accept that you will miss part of the main park. Check the hours of Ferrari Land for your date, since they have often been shorter.

faqs.q: How do you get to PortAventura from Barcelona by train?
faqs.a: Take a regional Rodalies train from Barcelona Sants or Passeig de Gràcia to the Port Aventura station. The journey takes about an hour and a half. Choose your return train in advance.

faqs.q: Does the PortAventura ticket include the water park?
faqs.a: No. Caribe Aquatic Park has a separate ticket and opens in summer only. Fast passes, lockers, parking and food are also extra.

faqs.q: How far is the Port Aventura train station from the park?
faqs.a: About a kilometre, along a signposted path to the gates.

title: Madrid with children: Parque Warner, the Parque de Atracciones, the zoo, Faunia or the aquarium, and how to get there without a car
subtitle: Five places built for children, two of them a metro ride from the centre and three at the edge of the city.
excerpt: Parque Warner, the Parque de Atracciones, the Zoo Aquarium, Faunia and Atlantis Aquarium: what each is, which age it suits, how long it takes, how to reach it by metro, train or bus, and what the tickets include.
secondary_keywords: Zoo Aquarium Madrid how to get there
longtail_phrases: how to get to Parque Warner from Madrid without a car
Parque Warner or Parque de Atracciones
Madrid zoo or Faunia
what to do in Madrid with a toddler
which metro goes to the Madrid zoo
meta_title: Madrid with children: which park, zoo or aquarium
meta_description: Parque Warner, the Parque de Atracciones, the zoo, Faunia or Atlantis Aquarium: which suits which age, and how to reach each one without a car.

featured_image.alt: A boat full of riders hits the water at the foot of a chute among red rocks at Parque Warner Madrid, throwing up a wall of spray

content_html:
[place attraction="parque-de-atracciones-de-madrid" city="madrid"]

When Philip II made Madrid his capital, he bought himself a hunting ground across the river from the palace. The Casa de Campo stayed a private estate of the crown for nearly four centuries. On 1 May 1931, two weeks after Spain became a republic, its gates were opened to the people of the city. Five years later the front line of the civil war ran through it, and the remains of trenches and bunkers are still there among the pines.

In 1969 an amusement park opened in the estate, and in 1972 the city zoo moved here from the Retiro park, where a royal menagerie had stood since the 1770s. So two of the five places Madrid has built for children are in the same great park, a few metro stops from the centre. The other three are at the edges of the city. Here is what each one is, which age it suits, and how to reach it without a car.

The five at a glance

  • Parque Warner: a film theme park with the biggest rides. South of the city. A full day.
  • Parque de Atracciones: the city's own amusement park, in the Casa de Campo. Half a day to a day.
  • Zoo Aquarium: a large zoo with an aquarium building, also in the Casa de Campo. Four to five hours.
  • Faunia: animals shown by habitat, much of it indoors. East of the centre. Three to four hours.
  • Atlantis Aquarium: a small aquarium inside a shopping centre, south-west of the city. An hour to an hour and a half.

Parque Warner

Opened in 2002 at San Martín de la Vega, about 30 kilometres from the centre. It has five areas: Hollywood Boulevard, Movie World Studios, DC Super Heroes World, Old West Territory and Cartoon Village. The coasters named after Superman and Batman, a wooden one and a tall drop tower are for older children and adults, and they have height limits. Cartoon Village is for the small ones. There is little shade, and in July the afternoon is very hot.

Without a car: the partner's listing gives the usual way. Take a Cercanías suburban train on line C-3 to Pinto, then bus 413 to the park gate. Allow well over an hour each way from the centre, and look up the last bus back before you go in.

Parque de Atracciones

Smaller and older than Warner, and inside the city. It mixes a traditional carousel and gentle rides with several serious coasters, and has an area themed on Nickelodeon cartoons for young children. Outside the summer and school holidays it opens mainly at weekends, so check the calendar.

Without a car: metro line 10 to Batán. The entrance is a few minutes on foot from the station.

The carousel of the Parque de Atracciones. Photo: Freddo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Zoo Aquarium

The zoo covers 22 hectares and groups its animals by continent. It has kept giant pandas since 1978, when a pair came as a gift from China, and a new young pair arrived in 2024. There are also koalas, gorillas, rhinos, an aviary, and a separate aquarium building with sharks. The ground is hilly in places and the distances are long for short legs: bring or hire a pushchair.

Without a car: metro line 5 or 10 to Casa de Campo, then a walk of about fifteen minutes through the park. A city bus from Príncipe Pío has run to the gate itself.

A giant panda at the zoo, photographed in 2009. Photo: Fernando Losada Rodríguez, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Faunia

Faunia opened in 2001 and works differently from a zoo. Instead of rows of enclosures it has pavilions that copy a habitat, which you walk through: a humid jungle with a staged tropical storm, a dark hall for nocturnal animals, and a polar hall where penguins of several species live on ice behind glass. Because so much is under a roof, it is the better choice on a very hot or a cold day. It is compact, which suits children under ten.

Without a car: metro line 9 to Valdebernardo, and a walk of about ten minutes.

Flamingos at Faunia. Photo: LBM1948, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Atlantis Aquarium

This aquarium is inside the Xanadú shopping centre at Arroyomolinos, about 25 kilometres south-west of Madrid. It shows sharks, rays, turtles, piranhas, penguins and jellyfish, and has virtual reality films. It is small. It works for toddlers and for a rainy day, and on its own it does not justify the journey. The same centre has an indoor ski slope, which makes the trip worth more.

Without a car: interurban buses leave from the Príncipe Pío interchange and stop at the shopping centre. Check the line and the timetable on the day.

Which one for which age

  • Under five: Faunia, or the zoo with a pushchair. Atlantis if it rains.
  • Five to nine: the zoo or the Parque de Atracciones.
  • Ten and over: Parque Warner if you can give it a whole day, the Parque de Atracciones if you cannot.
  • One free afternoon: the Parque de Atracciones or the zoo, because the metro takes you there.
  • Children of very different ages: the zoo. Nobody is too small or too tall for it.

What the tickets include

All five tickets our partner sells are plain entry tickets for a chosen date, shown on your phone. None comes with an audio guide or transport.

  • Parque Warner: all areas and rides. Not the passes that shorten ride queues, not food, and not the Halloween night event. The summer water park beside it has its own ticket.
  • Parque de Atracciones: the rides. Not the queue pass, and not the horror walk-through, which is charged separately.
  • Zoo Aquarium: entry and the daily talks with the keepers. Large bags go to a paid cloakroom.
  • Faunia: entry. The listing says it opens at 11:00 and that closing time changes with the date.
  • Atlantis Aquarium: entry without waiting at the ticket desk. Last admission is an hour before closing, and guided visits are sold on the spot, in Spanish only.

From here

The Casa de Campo itself costs nothing: its lake has rowing boats and a ring of cafés, one metro stop from the amusement park. Down by the river, the Madrid Río park has some of the best free playgrounds in the city. Hours are on our pages for the Parque de Atracciones, the Zoo Aquarium, Parque Warner and Faunia. See what else there is in Madrid, or open the trip planner for Spain.

The lake of the Casa de Campo, free to walk around. Photo: Kus Cámara, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Cover photo: Joseolgon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Parque Warner from Madrid without a car?
faqs.a: Take a Cercanías train on line C-3 to Pinto, then bus 413 to the park. Allow well over an hour each way and check the time of the last bus back.

faqs.q: Parque Warner or Parque de Atracciones: which is better?
faqs.a: Parque Warner is larger, with bigger rides and film themes, and needs a full day and a journey out of the city. The Parque de Atracciones is smaller, a few metro stops from the centre, and fits into half a day.

faqs.q: Madrid zoo or Faunia?
faqs.a: The zoo is bigger and has the famous animals, including giant pandas. Faunia is compact and largely indoors, with habitats you walk through, which suits small children and days of extreme weather.

faqs.q: What can you do in Madrid with a toddler?
faqs.a: Faunia and the Zoo Aquarium work well with a pushchair, Atlantis Aquarium is an indoor option for an hour, and the lake of the Casa de Campo and the playgrounds of Madrid Río are free.

faqs.q: Which metro goes to the Madrid zoo?
faqs.a: Lines 5 and 10 to Casa de Campo station, followed by a walk of about fifteen minutes through the park. Batán, on line 10, is the station for the Parque de Atracciones.

title: Valencia: the old town on foot and the Turia gardens by bike, what is free and what needs a ticket
subtitle: A compact medieval centre for walking, nine kilometres of park in a dry riverbed for cycling, and a short list of doors worth paying at.
excerpt: A walking loop through the old town of Valencia, what is free (the cathedral square, the Central Market, the Water Tribunal) and what needs a ticket (the cathedral, the Silk Exchange, the towers), and how to ride the Turia gardens from Bioparc to the City of Arts and Sciences.

meta_description: A walking loop through the old town of Valencia and a bike ride along the Turia gardens: what is free, what needs a ticket, and what each one includes.

featured_image.alt: The Plaza de la Virgen in Valencia with its fountain, the pink basilica of the Virgin and the Gothic door and bell tower of the cathedral

content_html:
[place attraction="valencia-cathedral" city="valencia"]

On 14 October 1957 the river Turia burst its banks twice in one day and put much of Valencia under water. At least 81 people died. The government's answer was to move the river: a new channel was dug around the south of the city, and by the early 1970s the old bed that curved through the middle of Valencia lay dry. The planners meant to fill it with a motorway.

The people of the city wanted something else. They campaigned under the slogan "the riverbed is ours and we want it green", and they won. From 1986 the bed was planted, stretch by stretch. Today it is a park about nine kilometres long, with a zoo at one end and the City of Arts and Sciences at the other, and old stone bridges crossing over nothing but trees. That gives a visit two halves: a small old town made for walking, and a long flat garden made for a bicycle.

The old town on foot

A loop of about three kilometres takes in the main sights. Allow two to three hours without going inside anything.

  • Start at the Torres de Serranos, the north gate of the medieval walls, built in the 1390s, which faces the riverbed.
  • Walk south to the Plaza de la Virgen and the cathedral.
  • Cross the Plaza de la Reina, past the Baroque tower of Santa Catalina and the round market square behind it.
  • Go on to the Lonja de la Seda and the Central Market, which face each other.
  • Finish at the town hall square, or turn west to the second surviving gate, the Torres de Quart, still pitted by cannon fire from 1808.

The Torres de Serranos, the north gate of the old walls. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is free

  • The Plaza de la Virgen. The square lies over the forum of the Roman city. The reclining figure in its fountain is the Turia, and the eight women around him are the irrigation channels that water the farmland outside the city.
  • The Water Tribunal. Every Thursday at noon, outside the Gothic door of the cathedral on this square, eight farmers in black smocks hold court on disputes over those channels. They rule on the spot, aloud, in Valencian, as their predecessors have done for many centuries. It lasts a few minutes and is open to anyone who arrives early enough to see.
  • The Central Market. A hall of iron, glass and tiles finished in 1928, with several hundred stalls. It is a working market, open in the morning and early afternoon and closed on Sundays. Go in, look up at the dome, and buy something.
  • The outsides. The cathedral has three doors in three styles, Romanesque, Gothic and Baroque. The alabaster doorway of the Palace of the Marqués de Dos Aguas is the most photographed in the city.
  • The Turia gardens, at any hour.

The dome of the Central Market, finished in 1928. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket

  • The cathedral. Visitors pay for a ticket that comes with an audio guide. People attending mass enter free. Inside are the chapel of the Holy Chalice, an agate cup venerated as the Holy Grail, two paintings by Goya, and Renaissance frescoes of angel musicians above the altar, uncovered in 2004.
  • The Miguelete, the cathedral's bell tower: 207 steps, and a small ticket of its own.
  • The Lonja de la Seda, the Silk Exchange, begun in 1482 and on the World Heritage list since 1996. Its trading hall is held up by twisted columns that open into the vault like palm trees. The ticket is one of the cheapest in the city, and the city has made entry free on Sundays and public holidays. Check that this still holds.
  • The two gate towers. You can climb both for a view over the roofs. They have followed the same rule as the Lonja.
  • The Hortensia Herrero Art Centre. A private collection of contemporary art, opened in 2023 in a restored palace near the cathedral, with works made for the building by artists such as Jaume Plensa and Olafur Eliasson.
  • Bioparc, the zoo at the western end of the gardens.

The Turia by bike

The gardens are flat, free of cars, and have a cycle path for their whole length. Rental shops are all over the old town.

  • West from the Torres de Serranos: about three and a half kilometres to the Cabecera park and Bioparc.
  • East: about four kilometres to the City of Arts and Sciences, past the concert hall and the Gulliver playground, a giant figure of Gulliver lying on his back that children climb over and slide down. It is free.

End to end, with stops, the ride fills half a day. One rule to know: in Spain it is forbidden to cycle with earphones in, and the fine is heavy. If you use an audio tour on a bike, stop to listen.

The Turia gardens, in the old bed of the river. Photo: Dorieo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Bioparc

Bioparc opened in 2008 and shows African animals only, in landscapes built to hide the barriers: a savannah with giraffes, rhinos and lions, an equatorial forest with gorillas, and a walk among the lemurs of Madagascar. The partner's listing notes that entry is by time slot, that you cannot go back in once you leave, and that children under four are free. Bicycles stay outside, in a free bike park. Allow three to four hours.

A gorilla at Bioparc, at the western end of the gardens. Photo: Alberto-g-rovi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What our partner sells here

  • The Old Town Audio Tour, up to two hours, starts at the town hall square and passes the market square, Santa Catalina and the cathedral.
  • The audio walk through the Old City Heart, two and a half hours, starts at the Torres de Serranos and ends at the Lonja. It is the closest to the loop above.
  • The Cultural Bike Tour is an audio route for cyclists through the Turia park and the centre. Bike hire is not included. A version with hire bundled in was not bookable when we looked.
  • The Hortensia Herrero ticket is entry with a multilingual audio guide.
  • The Bioparc ticket is entry by the fast lane.

The three audio products are commentary in the partner's app, on your own phone with your own earphones. No entry to any monument is included in them.

These are the walks, the bike route and the two tickets our partner sells here, with today's prices:

[partner city="valencia" match="town,heart,turia,hortensia,bioparc" limit="5"]

From here

At the eastern end of the gardens stands the City of Arts and Sciences, and the beach is a tram ride further. Hours are on our pages for Valencia Cathedral, the Lonja de la Seda and Bioparc. See what else there is in Valencia, or open the trip planner for Spain.

faqs.q: Is the Silk Exchange in Valencia free?
faqs.a: It has a small entry charge. The city has made it free on Sundays and public holidays, so check whether that still applies on your date.

faqs.q: How long are the Turia gardens?
faqs.a: About nine kilometres, in the old bed of the river, from the Cabecera park and Bioparc in the west to the City of Arts and Sciences in the east.

faqs.q: Can you cycle the Turia gardens?
faqs.a: Yes. They are flat and free of cars, with a cycle path for the whole length. Riding with earphones in is forbidden in Spain, so stop if you want to listen to an audio tour.

faqs.q: Is Valencia Cathedral free to enter?
faqs.a: Not for a tourist visit: there is a ticket, which comes with an audio guide. People attending mass enter free, and the bell tower has a separate ticket.

faqs.q: When does the Water Tribunal meet in Valencia?
faqs.a: On Thursdays at noon, outside the Gothic door of the cathedral on the Plaza de la Virgen. It is free to watch and lasts only a few minutes.
